title: Scaling peer support, counselling access, and stigma-reduction campaigns in Hong Kong secondary schools
reading_passage:
Role: Student welfare editor.
Audience: School wellness portal readers (students, parents).
Purpose: Write a discursive piece on whether peer listening programmes should be mandatory for senior forms, how to protect peer supporters, and how messaging can reduce stigma without minimising serious conditions.

Respect clinical boundaries; avoid giving instructions for crisis situations.
conceptual_explanation: Paper 2: sensitive topic register; balance of empathy and clarity; avoidance of harmful prescriptive medical advice while discussing policy.

full_marks_criteria: Content: nuanced treatment of peer support benefits/risks; HK school context.
Language: respectful lexis; modality for uncertainty; avoids harmful certainty claims.
Organisation: clear sections; ethical caveat where appropriate.
Does not trivialise serious mental illness nor demonise peer schemes.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 4)
interactive_tasks.answer:
Peer Listeners

Many schools have peer listeners now because counsellors are busy. Peers can help friends feel better but they are not doctors.

I think training is important. If peers work too much they may feel sad too. Schools should give rest time.

Messages should be kind and not scary words, but serious problems still need professionals.

Overall peer programmes are helpful if we are careful.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 5)
interactive_tasks.answer:
Peers Who Listen—Within Bounds

Scaling peer support is rational economics: adolescents often disclose to peers first. Rational ethics, however, demands supervision, triage scripts, and mandatory rotation so volunteers recover.

Mandatory senior participation could normalise help-seeking yet coerce introverts. Better: opt-in with incentives and transparent escalation maps—when silence is unsafe, how fast a counsellor joins.

Messaging should pair plain terminology in intake rooms with gentler assembly language—avoid both euphemism-only and shock-only framing.

Schools must fund release time for debriefs; compassion without logistics curdles into goodwill burnt on spreadsheets.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 5*)
interactive_tasks.answer:
Stigma Drops When Systems Work

Peer listeners are not mini-therapists; they are early routers on a care network. Mandate training, not gossip—not listening quotas scored like attendance.

Confidentiality charters audited by NGOs earn parent trust faster than inspirational videos. Publish aggregate referral latency KPIs—anonymised—so accountability is public without voyeurism.

Ethical guardrail: no chatbot-only pathway for ideation; technology queues, humans decide.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 5**)
interactive_tasks.answer:
The Architecture of Listening

Care is not a slogan laminated outside the counselling door; it is throughput architecture—how fast distress converts into competent response. I defend peer schemes only where supervision volume scales with caseload, and where silence for volunteers is scheduled as ruthlessly as exam drilling.

Our essays ask students to analyse tone; our wellbeing policy must analyse tone-deaf euphemisms. Say plainly what acute risk means in staff rooms; say softly in playgrounds only if soft language still routes urgency upward.

Measure what matters: referral accuracy drills, post-incident debrief completion, median hours to counsellor touch—not happiness hashtags.
